question.text: Mr. Aakash Verma, Fund Manager of Indus Cat III AIF — a long-only fund investing 100% in large-cap listed Indian equities (blue-chip focus) — must state the benchmark in the PPM. The fund does NOT use leverage and does NOT take short positions. Which benchmark is MOST appropriate per Example 10.7 of Chapter 10?

answer.text: NIFTY 50 TRI or S&P BSE SENSEX TRI — broad-based large-cap free-float market-cap-weighted indices; Total Return variant chosen so dividend accrual is captured in the comparison.
A fixed 10% p.a. hurdle rate, since all Cat III AIFs must use absolute-return benchmarking.
NIFTY Small Cap 100, because the fund is a Category III AIF and Cat III always benchmarks to small-caps.
CRISIL Composite Bond Index, because Cat III AIFs must always use a debt benchmark to reflect capital preservation.

explanation.text: The Logic: Per Example 10.7 Fund X (large-cap long-only listed equities), appropriate benchmarks are NIFTY 50, S&P BSE Sensex, NIFTY Next 50, BSE Next 50, NIFTY 100, or S&P BSE 100. The TRI variant is preferred per Section 10.5.6 so dividends are captured — matching pre-tax NAV reporting. The Trap: Option B misapplies 'absolute-return' (reserved for market-neutral / leveraged / concentrated Cat III strategies) to a long-only fund. Options C and D attach the wrong asset class entirely. Cross-Exam Context: XXI-B (PM) tests benchmark selection for listed portfolios. XIX-C extends to AIF-specific situations including absolute-return strategies. Manager's Pro-Tip: Always specify the TRI (Total Return Index) variant in your PPM, not the price index. Using price index inflates apparent alpha by ~1.5-2% p.a. on Indian large-caps — a savvy LP catches this and penalises the GP during fee negotiations.
